title: Square and Triangle
context: Grade 5, the pages on the perimeters of squares and triangles and Exercise 8.1. An adult sees two formulas and two harder questions. What the pages are doing is adding equal sides quickly and working back: a square's four equal sides make 4 x side, a triangle's three sides are simply added, and half a rectangle's perimeter is one length and one breadth together.

writeup.why: Find the perimeter of a square as 4 x side and of a triangle as the sum of its sides, work back to a rectangle's length by halving its perimeter, and find the distance of several laps, with a side in tenths read as tenths.
writeup.look: A square, a triangle or a rectangle on squared paper, a Sum strip under it, a perimeter string on the third phase, and a square path with a lap counter and the Tenths lens on the last.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Square and Triangle' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number of sides added, or on the last phase the laps walked. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The figure lies on squared paper at x 120, y 230 inside a box 560 by 380, drawn to one scale, its given sides labelled deep blue. The Copy side and Times 4 buttons stand at x 760, y 250 and x 760, y 330. The ant walks the boundary, each side lighting vermilion, labelled Boundary, and dropping its length into the Sum strip along y 650 from x 120. On the third phase the perimeter string lies straight at y 600, 820 long, vermilion, and the Halve button at x 760, y 420 folds it; the half lays itself along one length and one breadth of the rectangle, and the Take away tile at x 760, y 500 lifts the breadth off, leaving the length green. On the fourth phase the Tenths lens is a round glass 90 across that shows a side as a count of tenths, and the Lap button and lap counter stand at x 760, y 420. The answer reached is green. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with a point key, a cm key and an m key. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the ten tools of this chapter share them. The lengths the question gives, as a side, a length, a breadth, a height, an edge or a base area, are deep blue, labelled Given or by their own name. The perimeter, area, volume or missing side the working reaches is green, labelled Answer. The boundary that a perimeter walks round is vermilion, labelled Boundary. The unit being counted, one unit square, one unit cube, one row or one layer, is violet, labelled Unit square, Unit cube, Row or Layer. The part squares of an estimate and the space left over where no whole cube fits are rose, labelled More than half, Half or Left over. The side, square, cube, layer or step being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open, and nothing on this stage is ever grey. A square or cube that is not being counted stays warm white inside its near-black outline, grid lines, unit words and signs are near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The last figure stays drawn with its boundary vermilion, and the working line under it ends on the answer in green with its unit.

writeup.delight: On the third phase, when the halved string settles along one length and one breadth, the folded half gives a small wave along its whole length and then lies still.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet tapped. On the first phase a square lies with one side labelled and three blank, the Copy side button beside it. On the second a triangle lies with its three sides labelled and the ant at a corner. On the third a rectangle lies with its breadth labelled, its length blank, and a vermilion perimeter string laid out beside it. On the fourth a square path lies with the Tenths lens and the Lap button beside it. One thing moves, once: the Copy side button, the ant, the string or the Lap button gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.
writeup.freePlay: Any square, triangle or rectangle along the grid lines, halved, lapped or read through the Tenths lens. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on squares, triangles, a length worked back from a perimeter, and laps.

source_tool.description: A figure lies on squared paper, drawn to one scale, its given sides labelled deep blue. For a square, the child taps one side and a Copy side button lays its length on the other three, then a Times 4 button folds the four into 4 x side. For a triangle, the child walks an ant round the three sides, each lighting vermilion, labelled Boundary, and dropping its length into a Sum strip. For working back, a rectangle's perimeter is laid out as a vermilion string beside it; a Halve button folds the string in half and lays the half along one length and one breadth, and a Take away tile lifts the breadth off the half, leaving the length in green. On the last phase a Lap button sends the ant once round a square path per tap, and a lap counter adds one lap each time; a Tenths lens rewrites a side in tenths of a metre as a count of tenths and writes the total back in metres. A number pad types a length with its unit. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of sides added, or the laps walked.
source_tool.art_direction: A chalk square in the schoolyard / Picture book

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: squared paper with equal square cells, rulers marked in centimetres, unit cubes that stack into rows, layers and cuboids, open boxes, and clear jars of water with a level line.
Every figure is drawn to one scale inside its stage, so a side twice as long looks twice as long, and every square cell and every unit cube in one picture is the same size.
Every side, edge and measure carries its unit: cm or m for a length, sq. cm or sq. m for an area, and cu. cm or cu. m for a volume. The longer side of a rectangle is always the one labelled length.
A cuboid is drawn in three visible faces, and a cube only when all its edges are equal. Cubes hidden behind or under others are shown by a see-through layer when they are counted.
A part square on an estimate is marked by its kind, more than half, half or less than half, in words; no cross ever marks a square that is counted.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: a walker tracing a boundary, rows of squares filling a rectangle, layers of cubes stacking into a cuboid, or water rising in a jar.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a square, a cube or a number the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a measure plays in a piece of working: the lengths the question gives, as a side, a length, a breadth, a height, an edge or a base area, are deep blue, and the perimeter, area, volume or missing side the working reaches is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The boundary that a perimeter walks round is vermilion. The unit being counted, one unit square, one unit cube, one row or one layer, is violet. The part squares an area estimate rounds, and the space left over where no whole cube fits, are rose. The side, square, cube, layer or step being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open and is not used here. A square or cube that is not being counted stays warm white inside its outline, and grid lines and unit words are near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Boundary, Unit square, Unit cube, Layer, More than half, Half and Left over, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Walk it once more. Did every side, or every lap, go in?
voice.onNext: A new shape. Look at its sides first.
voice.opening: A shape on squared paper, ready to walk.
voice.onFinish: You added equal sides quickly and worked back to a side.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Make squares, triangles and laps of your own.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has chalked a square on the ground, measured one side and walked a lap. The tool is what folds a perimeter string in half onto one length and one breadth, which paper can only describe.

answer_key.rule: A square has four equal sides, so its perimeter is 4 x side. A triangle's perimeter is the sum of its three sides, all in one unit. Half a rectangle's perimeter is one length and one breadth together, so the length is half the perimeter take away the breadth; check by 2 x (length + breadth). Going round several times is one lap multiplied by the number of laps. A side in tenths is a count of tenths: multiply the count by a whole number, then write the answer back in metres.
answer_key.wrong: The ant walks the figure again beside the child's answer, adding each side as it goes, and the side, the half or the lap the child left out or counted twice is lit amber. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: All four sides of a square are equal, so every side is 19 cm.
Four equal sides make 4 x side: 4 x 19 = 76.
So the perimeter of a square of side 19 cm is 4 x 19 = 76 cm.
items.question: A square tile has sides of 19 cm. What is its perimeter?
items.checkpoint: Four equal sides, so four lots of one side.
items.misconception: Taking two lots of the side, as for one length and one breadth, which walks only half way round.

steps: Walk the three sides once each: 13 cm, 15 cm and 17 cm.
So the perimeter of a triangle with sides 13 cm, 15 cm and 17 cm is 45 cm.
items.question: A triangle has sides of 13 cm, 15 cm and 17 cm. What is its perimeter?
items.checkpoint: A triangle's perimeter is its three sides added.
items.misconception: Adding only two of the sides, which leaves part of the boundary out.

steps: Half the perimeter is 18 cm, because 2 x 18 = 36.
That half is one length and one breadth together.
items.question: A rectangle has a perimeter of 36 cm and a breadth of 7 cm. How long is it?
items.checkpoint: Halve first, then take the breadth away.
items.misconception: Taking the breadth away from the whole perimeter instead of from half of it, which leaves two lengths and a breadth mixed together.

steps: 3.4 m is 34 tenths of a metre.
One lap is four sides: 4 x 34 = 136, so one lap is 136 tenths, which is 13.6 m.
Five laps: 5 x 136 = 680, so 680 tenths, which is 68 m.
items.question: A square pond path has sides of 3.4 m. How far is 5 times round it?
items.checkpoint: Find one lap first, then multiply by the number of laps.
items.misconception: Forgetting that 34 counts tenths of a metre, and giving an answer ten times too big.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: A square card has sides of 9 cm. What is its perimeter?
A triangle has sides of 5 cm, 7 cm and 9 cm. What is its perimeter?
A rectangle has a perimeter of 20 cm and a breadth of 3 cm. How long is it?
items.final_answer: Half of 20 is 10, and 10 - 3 = 7, so the length is 7 cm

items.question: A square frame has sides of 23 cm. What is its perimeter?
A triangle has sides of 1 m, 80 cm and 65 cm. What is its perimeter in cm?
One lap round a field is 45 m. How far are 3 laps?
A rectangle has a perimeter of 50 m and a breadth of 9 m. How long is it?
items.final_answer: Half of 50 is 25, and 25 - 9 = 16, so the length is 16 m

items.question: A square path has sides of 2.6 m. How far is 3 times round it?
items.final_answer: 2.6 m is 26 tenths. One lap is 4 x 26 = 104 tenths, which is 10.4 m. Three laps are 3 x 104 = 312 tenths, which is 31.2 m

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

teaching_notes: Chalk a square on the ground, measure one side and walk a lap before the tool opens. A square's four equal sides make 4 x side; check it once by adding all four. A triangle has no formula to learn: add its three sides in one unit. To work back to a side, halve the perimeter first, and say that the half is one length and one breadth together. For laps, find one lap first. Read a side in tenths as a count of tenths, multiply by a whole number, and write the answer back in metres; a decimal is never multiplied by a decimal here. The printed sides and parks are the child's to work.
generation_prompt: Build a square and triangle perimeter tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. Figures are drawn to one scale on squared paper, given sides labelled deep blue. A Copy side button lays one side of a square on the other three and a Times 4 button folds them into 4 x side. An ant walks a triangle's three sides into a Sum strip, each side lighting vermilion, labelled Boundary. For working back, a rectangle's perimeter is a vermilion string; a Halve button folds it in half along one length and one breadth, and a Take away tile lifts the breadth off, leaving the length in green. A Lap button sends the ant once round a square path per tap with a lap counter, and a Tenths lens reads a side in tenths of a metre as a count of tenths. A number pad types lengths with cm, m and point keys. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the sides added or the laps walked. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Copy one side of the square onto the others. Halve a perimeter to find one length and one breadth. Find one lap before counting laps.
